extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent prosecutors, and analysts who use examiner statistics to plan prosecution strategy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for measuring and comparing USPTO examiner difficulty using grant-rate statistics (e.g., backward grant rate, three-year grant rate) and timelines; includes how to construct timelines, interpret differences, and caveats when using these metrics to plan prosecution. Useful for selecting prosecution tactics (RCE vs appeal) and explaining probabilities to clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backward grant rate
rubrics_metrics.description: The commonly used statistic that looks backward to tell you what percentage of applications that have already been disposed were granted (granted/(granted + abandoned)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful as a simple historical summary of disposed cases, but it is backward‑looking and can be influenced by applicant behavior (assiduousness) and abandonment rates; may assign the same difficulty level to examiners whose underlying timelines differ substantially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-year grant rate (3YGR)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'three-year grant rate' that shows the probability of obtaining a granted patent within three years of the first office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a single-number summary of examiner difficulty and expected time-to-issue; chosen because three years balances allowing meaningful prosecution while remaining a near-term measure. Less influenced by applicant assiduousness than the backward grant rate and can better reflect examiner difficulty in many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant rate timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: A timeline that shows your chances of being granted a patent at different times after receiving your first office action and also the percentages of abandoned and pending applications at those same intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides richer information than a single number: shows when grants/abandonments occur, reveals patterns such as whether an examiner is difficult before or after an RCE, and can inform tactical decisions. The full timeline should be used to plan prosecution strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeline construction method
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct timelines by taking all patent applications and shifting them so the dates of their first office actions are the same; then, for each month afterwards, compute the percentage of patent applications that were granted, still pending, or abandoned by that month.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method is straightforward but involves 'time travel' effects: for large datasets grant and abandonment rates increase over time. Be aware that the number of cases declines on the right side of the timeline, producing greater variability there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use full timeline for prosecution strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage the full grant-rate timeline (not just a single-number rate) to plan prosecution strategy such as whether to file an RCE or a notice of appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timelines can show examiners who become easier after an RCE or who make an early decision that's hard to change later; use these patterns to choose the most cost-effective path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment rate as a separate signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandonment rates at a given time (e.g., three years) can differ markedly between examiners and reflect factors like applicant willingness to continue prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences in abandonment (not just grants) explain why backward grant rate and 3YGR can tell different stories; interpret examiner difficulty by separating inherent examiner behavior from applicant-driven abandonment (example: DY vs BG).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size and timeline variability caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of cases at later timeline points is much smaller than at the start, so grant and abandonment rates on the right side of the timeline have greater variability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret late-time percentages cautiously; the blog gives an example (DY had 141 cases at year 0 and 40 cases at year 4) to illustrate increased variability with fewer observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude SPEs and small-N examiners from certain comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing metrics like backward grant rate and 3YGR across examiners, exclude SPEs and examiners with a small number of cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing these outliers helps produce more meaningful correlations and comparisons between metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors influencing grant rates unrelated to examiner merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-examiner factors that influence grant or abandonment rates include the nature of the technology, mostly random assignment of cases, influence of a primary examiner or SPE, and applicant behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize these confounders when interpreting grant-rate metrics; numbers can misrepresent an examiner's inherent difficulty if these factors are not considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of timeframe for grant-rate window
rubrics_metrics.description: The precise time window (three years in this article) is somewhat arbitrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three years was selected as a balance between providing enough time for meaningful prosecution and obtaining a relatively near-term measure; other windows could be chosen depending on analysis goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation and systematic differences between metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: The backward grant rate and the three-year grant rate are highly correlated with each other, with the backward grant rate being on average a little higher than the three-year grant rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correlation does not eliminate important cases where the two metrics diverge (e.g., same backward rate but very different 3YGR), so examine timelines to detect such divergences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical/cautionary note on assigning numeric ratings to people
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an inherent unfairness in assigning a number to a person; many examiners work hard and factors outside their control influence grant rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using statistics, look beyond the numbers and consider context before making qualitative judgments about examiner performance.
